primer.ane_p_world.title: The great kingdoms
primer.ane_p_world.text: You were born in the age of the great Bronze Age kingdoms. Pharaonic Egypt, Kassite Babylon, Assyria, the Hittites in Anatolia and Mitanni on the Euphrates fight, trade and write each other letters on clay tablets in Akkadian, the language of diplomacy. Kings call one another “brother” and swap gold, horses, lapis lazuli and brides. Beneath them millions of farmers till the land along the Nile, the Tigris and the Euphrates. Around 1200 BC this whole world will be shaken by invasions, famine and falling kingdoms.
primer.ane_p_world_eg_rise.title: An empire is born
primer.ane_p_world_eg_rise.text: Around 1550 BC King Ahmose I of Thebes drove out the Hyksos, foreigners who had ruled northern Egypt for a century, and reunited the land. So began the New Kingdom. His successors march south into Nubia for gold and north into Syria: Thutmose I reached the Euphrates, Queen Hatshepsut rules as pharaoh, shown on her statues with the ritual beard, and sends ships to the land of Punt for incense. Thutmose III led some seventeen campaigns and smashed a coalition of Syrian princes at Megiddo.
primer.ane_p_world_eg_gold.title: The golden age
primer.ane_p_world_eg_gold.text: Egypt is at the peak of its wealth: gold comes from Nubia, tribute from Syria, and the kings of Babylon and Mitanni send the pharaoh their daughters as wives while begging for gold, “for in your land it is as plentiful as dust”. Amenhotep II and Thutmose IV still go to war, but Amenhotep III (c. 1390–1352) reigns in peace for nearly forty years and builds: Luxor Temple and a vast mortuary temple guarded by two stone colossi as tall as a six-storey house. His chief wife Tiye is not of royal birth, yet corresponds with kings herself.
primer.ane_p_world_eg_amarna.title: The heretic pharaoh
primer.ane_p_world_eg_amarna.text: Pharaoh Amenhotep IV renamed himself Akhenaten, “effective for the Aten”, and raised the sun disc, the Aten, above all other gods. Amun’s temples are shut, his name is chiselled off the walls, and the court has moved to a new capital, Akhetaten, built in the desert. After Akhenaten died around 1336 BC, the boy king Tutankhamun restored the old gods and the old capitals. Then the throne passes to the courtier Ay and the general Horemheb, who restores order with harsh decrees against corrupt officials.
primer.ane_p_world_eg_ramesses.title: The age of Ramesses
primer.ane_p_world_eg_ramesses.text: A new dynasty of soldiers holds the throne: Seti I and his son Ramesses II (1279–1213 BC), who reigns for 66 years. Ramesses fought the Hittites at Kadesh in 1274 and proclaimed a great victory, though the battle was really a draw; some fifteen years later he signed one of the earliest known peace treaties with the Hittite king. He builds Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum and a new capital, Pi-Ramesses, in the Delta, and fathers more than a hundred children. His son Merneptah beats back the Libyans and the “Sea Peoples”.
primer.ane_p_world_eg_decline.title: The New Kingdom fades
primer.ane_p_world_eg_decline.text: Ramesses III (c. 1184–1153 BC) repelled an invasion by the Sea Peoples, wrecking their ships in the Nile mouths, but the treasury is running dry. Around 1156 the craftsmen who cut the royal tombs went unpaid in grain and laid down their tools, the first strike on record. Bread grows dear, Libyans raid villages, and thieves break into the tombs of pharaohs, their trials written down on papyrus. Under the last Ramesses, the Eleventh, the country is effectively split between the High Priest of Amun at Thebes and a ruler in the Delta.
primer.ane_p_world_bab_kassite.title: Kassite Babylon
primer.ane_p_world_bab_kassite.text: After the Hittites sacked Babylon in 1595 BC, the city was taken by the Kassites, newcomers from the Zagros mountains. They leave the old order intact: they worship Marduk, write in Akkadian, and their kingdom of Karduniash unites all of southern Mesopotamia once more. Kings like Kurigalzu and Burnaburiash build temples and new cities and write to the pharaohs, angling for gold and exchanging daughters. Babylon is rich and calm, though a dangerous neighbour is growing strong in the north: Assyria.
primer.ane_p_world_bab_troubles.title: Babylon’s troubled century
primer.ane_p_world_bab_troubles.text: Around 1225 BC the Assyrian king Tukulti-Ninurta I captured Babylon, led its king away in chains and carried off the statue of Marduk. The Kassites regained power, but around 1155 the Elamites struck from the east, looting cities, hauling the stele of Hammurabi’s laws off to Susa and seizing Marduk once again. A new dynasty from Isin revived the land: Nebuchadnezzar I (c. 1125–1104) defeated Elam and brought the god home in triumph. Meanwhile Aramean tribes are roaming the steppe.
primer.ane_p_world_assur_mitanni.title: Under Mitanni’s thumb
primer.ane_p_world_assur_mitanni.text: Assur is still a small city-state on a rock above the Tigris. It remembers the days when its merchants led donkey caravans laden with tin and cloth all the way to Anatolia, but now Mitanni, a Hurrian kingdom of chariot lords, holds sway over it. The Mitannian king Saushtatar, one treaty records, carried off doors of gold and silver from Assur. The rulers of Assur pay tribute, bide their time and pray to the god Ashur, whose name the city bears.
primer.ane_p_world_assur_rise.title: Assyria rises
primer.ane_p_world_assur_rise.text: King Ashur-uballit I (c. 1363–1328 BC) threw off Mitanni’s rule and wrote to the pharaoh as an equal, calling him “brother”, to the fury of the Babylonian king, who considered the Assyrians his subjects. His heirs Adad-nirari I and Shalmaneser I crushed Mitanni and took its lands up to the Euphrates. Tukulti-Ninurta I (c. 1243–1207) defeated the Hittites, captured Babylon and built himself a new capital across the Tigris. Assyrians are known for their harshness: captives are deported and resettled by the thousand.
primer.ane_p_world_assur_tiglath.title: Collapse and revival
primer.ane_p_world_assur_tiglath.text: Tukulti-Ninurta was murdered by his own son and nobles, and Assyria faded for a century: its lands shrank, Aramean tribes raided from the west, and the world around was crumbling, with the Hittite empire gone and the cities of Syria in ruins. But Tiglath-pileser I (c. 1114–1076 BC) raised the kingdom up again: he claims he reached the Mediterranean, put out to sea in a ship and killed a “sea horse”, perhaps a whale. He boasts of slaying hundreds of lions and plants his gardens with trees from conquered lands.
primer.ane_p_place.title: Lands of the rivers
primer.ane_p_place.text: Your world is a set of river valleys in the desert: the Nile in Egypt, the Tigris and Euphrates in Mesopotamia. Without the river there is no life here; rain is scarce or absent, and every field is watered by the flood or a canal. Where the water stops, the sand and the steppe begin, roamed by shepherds and their flocks. Towns hug the water’s edge, and the main road is the river, carrying boats loaded with grain, stone, cattle and people.
primer.ane_p_place_thebes.title: Thebes, city of Amun
primer.ane_p_place_thebes.text: Thebes, Waset to Egyptians, spreads along both banks of the Nile. On the east bank lies the city of the living and Karnak, the vast temple of Amun, where every pharaoh adds new gateways and gold-capped obelisks; an avenue of sphinxes leads to Luxor Temple. On the west bank lies the city of the dead: mortuary temples, nobles’ tombs, the Valley of the Kings hidden in the cliffs, and Deir el-Medina, the village of the craftsmen who carve those tombs. The air smells of river mud, incense, fresh bread and lotus flowers.
primer.ane_p_place_memphis.title: Memphis of the White Walls
primer.ane_p_place_memphis.text: Memphis is Egypt’s oldest capital; its ancient name, Inbu-hedj, means “White Walls”. Here stands the great temple of Ptah, the craftsman god and patron of artisans, and in a shrine of his own lives the sacred Apis bull. The north of the country is run from here, with its vizier, scribes and arsenals, while in the harbour of Peru-nefer shipwrights build warships and dockers unload cedar from Byblos and copper from Cyprus. To the west, on the desert’s edge, lie Saqqara and the pyramids of Giza, already more than a thousand years old.
primer.ane_p_place_babylon.title: Babylon, Gate of God
primer.ane_p_place_babylon.text: Babylon, Bab-ilim or “Gate of God”, sits on the Euphrates in a flat plain criss-crossed by canals. Above its walls and gates rises the Esagila, Marduk’s temple, “the house whose top is high”. The streets are narrow and crooked, and mud-brick houses turn blank walls to the street, facing inward onto courtyards. Beyond the city lie date groves, barley fields and reed marshes full of wild boar and ducks. In summer it tops forty degrees and the wind carries dust, and Babylon’s scribes are famous throughout the world.
primer.ane_p_place_assur.title: Assur on the rock
primer.ane_p_place_assur.text: Assur stands on a rocky headland above the Tigris: the river guards it on two sides, massive walls on the rest. On the highest point rise the temple of the god Ashur and a stepped tower, the ziggurat, with the royal palace nearby. Below stretch the steppe, where sheep graze, and narrow barley fields along the river. Temple and family archives hold thousands of tablets: contracts, accounts, letters and the stern Assyrian laws. In the 13th century BC a new royal capital, Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta, will rise on the opposite bank.
primer.ane_p_society.title: King, scribes and ploughmen
primer.ane_p_society.text: At the top stands the king, the gods’ deputy on earth; below him come nobles, priests, scribes and chariot warriors. Everything rests on the farmers, who work land belonging to temples, the crown and the nobility and hand over a large share of the crop. There are slaves, war captives and debtors, but relatively few; big projects are done by free people as labour duty. A scribe who can read hieroglyphs or cuneiform ranks above any ploughman: “Be a scribe, it will save you from toil,” Egyptian teaching texts advise.
primer.ane_p_society_slave.title: In bondage
primer.ane_p_society_slave.text: You were born in bondage. Slaves here are captives from campaigns, as pharaohs bring back thousands of people from Syria and Nubia and Assyrians drive off whole villages, or debtors who sold themselves or their children. Slaves are given to temples, awarded to soldiers for bravery, hired out by the day. In Egypt a slave may own a few things and marry a free woman, and a master can free him or even adopt him. In Mesopotamia slaves were long marked out by a special hairstyle or brand.
primer.ane_p_society_peasant.title: A ploughman by the river
primer.ane_p_society_peasant.text: You were born into a farming family, like nearly everyone around you. Your land most likely belongs to a temple, the king or a noble, and a hefty share of the harvest goes to them. In Egypt scribes arrive before the harvest, measure the field with a rope and reckon the tax in grain; those who fall short are beaten with sticks. There is labour duty too: clearing canals and hauling stone for building projects. In Mesopotamia water is on everyone’s mind all year: let a canal silt up and the field turns salty and dies.
primer.ane_p_society_noble.title: Close to the throne
primer.ane_p_society_noble.text: You were born into a family close to the throne. Noble houses own estates and keep scribes, servants and chariots; in Egypt their sons are raised at court alongside the princes and called “children of the nursery”. Posts such as vizier, high priest or army commander often pass from father to son. But all favour flows from the king: the pharaoh rewards the loyal with the “gold of honour”, heavy golden collars, and can strip a man of everything for a single betrayal.
primer.ane_p_birth.title: Birth bricks
primer.ane_p_birth.text: An Egyptian woman gives birth squatting on two bricks, embodied by the goddess Meskhenet, who also decides the newborn’s fate. Midwives attend her, while Bes and Taweret, painted on walls and carved on amulets, chase off evil spirits. The child is named at once, often after a god: Amenhotep means “Amun is content”. In Mesopotamia the great dread is Lamashtu, a demoness who steals babies, so people recite spells and hang amulets against her. Childbirth here is mortally dangerous for mother and child alike.
primer.ane_p_childhood.title: Childhood by the river
primer.ane_p_childhood.text: Your mother nurses you until about three, just as Egyptian wisdom texts recommend. After that childhood happens in the yard and the fields: leapfrog, balls of leather and papyrus, wooden dolls and animal toys with jaws that snap. From about five there is work: herding geese, fetching water, minding goats. Older boys learn their father’s trade. Children of the elite and future scribes go to school, at a temple or palace in Egypt, or to a scribe’s “tablet house” in Mesopotamia.
primer.ane_p_home.title: A house of mud
primer.ane_p_home.text: In Egypt and Mesopotamia alike, houses are built of mud brick, clay mixed with straw and dried in the sun; stone is kept for temples and tombs. A farmer’s house has two or three rooms, a hearth, a storeroom full of grain jars and a flat roof for drying dates and sleeping on hot nights. Furniture is sparse: mats, chests, low stools, and for the rich, beds on legs carved like animal paws. In the evening a clay lamp burns sesame or castor oil.
primer.ane_p_food.title: Bread and beer
primer.ane_p_food.text: The staples are bread and beer: thick, cloudy barley beer is drunk by everyone from children to the king, and workers are even paid in rations of bread and beer. Alongside come onions, garlic, lentils, cucumbers, dates and river fish, with goose and beef for the rich. Egyptians love figs and honey cakes; Mesopotamians, sesame oil and date syrup. Wine is a luxury for the elite and for festivals, and the jars are labelled with the vineyard and the vintage year.
primer.ane_p_clothes.title: Linen and wool
primer.ane_p_clothes.text: Egyptians dress in white linen: men in loincloths and short kilts, women in close-fitting dresses, and the rich in gauzy pleated cloth you can almost see through. Children run around naked until their teens. Eyes are lined with green or black paint, for beauty and against sun and flies. In Mesopotamia people wear wool: long fringed tunics and shawls, and men grow beards. The elite drip with gold, carnelian and lapis lazuli, and in Egypt they wear wigs as well.
primer.ane_p_faith.title: Gods and temples
primer.ane_p_faith.text: Every city here belongs to its god: Thebes to Amun, Memphis to Ptah, Babylon to Marduk, Assur to the god Ashur. The god lives in his temple as a statue: each morning priests wake him, wash him, dress him and feed him, and ordinary people see him only at festivals, when the statue is carried out in a boat-shrine or on a litter. At home people pray to humbler guardian spirits, wear amulets and fear the demons of disease. The future is read in dreams, oracles and the liver of a sacrificed lamb.
primer.ane_p_faith_egypt.title: The gods of Egypt
primer.ane_p_faith_egypt.text: Egyptians believe the world rests on Maat, order and truth, and that the pharaoh keeps it from collapse by serving the gods. The state’s chief god is Amun-Ra, “king of the gods”; beside him stand Osiris, judge of the dead, Isis, Hathor and Ptah. At home people honour the dwarf god Bes and the hippo goddess Taweret, protectors of mothers and children. After death your heart is weighed against the feather of Maat, and to pass that judgement the wealthy take a Book of the Dead, a scroll of spells, into the tomb.
primer.ane_p_faith_meso.title: The gods of Mesopotamia
primer.ane_p_faith_meso.text: The gods of Mesopotamia eat, drink, rage and quarrel just like people, and humans, the myths say, were made to do the gods’ work for them. Babylon’s chief god is Marduk, Assyria’s is Ashur; there are also Shamash, the sun and judge, Sin the moon, Ishtar, goddess of love and war, and Adad, lord of storms. Everyone has a personal god to speak up for them. Diviners called baru read the gods’ will in a lamb’s liver, and exorcists drive out the demons of disease. The underworld is a dark “house of dust” from which no one returns.
primer.ane_p_faith_meso_memphis.title: Foreign gods in Memphis
primer.ane_p_faith_meso_memphis.text: Your family comes from the newcomers from the east, of whom Memphis has plenty: merchants, shipmen, craftsmen and the descendants of captives. By the harbour of Peru-nefer there are even shrines to Baal and Astarte, and Egyptians themselves pray to these gods, seeing in Baal a likeness of Seth. At home you call on your own gods in your own tongue and swear by their names. Yet over time many such families take Egyptian names, serve Ptah and bury their dead the Egyptian way, with amulets and prayers to Osiris.
primer.ane_p_work.title: Copper, grain and silver
primer.ane_p_work.text: There are no coins yet. Prices are reckoned in measures of grain, in Egypt also in deben (a deben is about 91 grams of copper), in Mesopotamia in shekels of silver weighing about 8 grams, and in Kassite Babylon even in gold. People pay with whatever they have: an ox might cost some cloth, jars of oil and bronze vessels, all totted up in deben. Workers are paid rations of grain. Merchants bring copper from Cyprus, cedar from Lebanon, tin from the east and lapis lazuli from distant mountains beyond Iran.
primer.ane_p_law.title: Justice and truth
primer.ane_p_law.text: In Egypt justice is done by the vizier and by local councils, the kenbet, made up of respected men; sometimes an oracle decides: the statue of Amun is carried on a litter and “nods” towards the party in the right. Punishments are harsh: beatings, a cut-off nose, exile to the mines, and death for robbing royal tombs. Mesopotamia still remembers Hammurabi’s laws, and the Assyrian laws of this age are especially brutal: many offences bring flogging, mutilation and forced labour for the king.
primer.ane_p_health.title: Healers and spells
primer.ane_p_health.text: A healer here is doctor and spell-caster in one. Egyptian physicians are famous everywhere, and foreign kings ask for them to be sent to their courts; they set bones, stitch wounds and dress them with honey to keep them from festering. Papyri list hundreds of remedies, from garlic to mouse fat. In Mesopotamia the asu treats patients with herbs while the ashipu drives out the demon that sent the illness. Eye diseases, worms, fevers and childbirth carry many off; reaching forty counts as good luck.
primer.ane_p_women.title: Women of the river lands
primer.ane_p_women.text: Girls are married young, at around 13 to 15, by agreement between families, and the husband is usually older; the bride brings a dowry of cloth, household goods and jewellery that remains her own. The mistress of the house runs the storerooms, raises the children, spins, weaves, brews beer and bakes bread. A woman of rank may become a priestess or a temple singer and manage an estate, and queens keep up their own correspondence. Childlessness is the greatest sorrow, and a husband may take a second wife or a concubine.
primer.ane_p_women_egypt.title: Mistress of the house
primer.ane_p_women_egypt.text: An Egyptian woman, the nebet-per or “mistress of the house”, is nearly a man’s equal before the law: she owns land, buys and sells, testifies in court, inherits and writes her own will. One woman of the craftsmen’s village at Deir el-Medina even disinherited the children who had neglected her in old age. Marriage simply means living under one roof; divorce is possible, and a third of the shared property stays with the wife. Noblewomen serve as singers of Amun, and Hatshepsut ruled as pharaoh.
primer.ane_p_women_meso.title: Women of Mesopotamia
primer.ane_p_women_meso.text: In Mesopotamia a bride moves into her husband’s house in exchange for a bride-price and with a dowry. In Babylon a woman may own property and do business, widows especially. Assyrian laws are severe: a married woman must cover her head in public, while slave women and prostitutes are forbidden to veil on pain of punishment, and a husband may legally beat a wife who has done wrong. Noblewomen and priestesses enjoy more freedom, and queens and princesses have their own quarters and households with scribes and servants.
primer.ane_p_leisure.title: Festivals and games
primer.ane_p_leisure.text: The happiest times are temple festivals. At the Opet festival in Thebes the statue of Amun sails by boat to Luxor Temple, and in Mesopotamia spring brings the New Year festival, Akitu. Bread, beer and sacrificial meat are handed out to the crowds. At home people play board games: the Egyptian senet with its 30 squares and the “game of twenty squares”. Musicians play harps, lutes and sistrums, and dancers tumble and sing. The elite hunt ducks in the reeds and lions on the steppe.
primer.ane_p_knowledge.title: Scribes and tablets
primer.ane_p_knowledge.text: Learning to write takes years. An Egyptian pupil copies wisdom texts onto potsherds and wooden boards, memorises hundreds of hieroglyphs and the cursive hieratic, and for laziness, as the saying goes, “a boy’s ear is on his back: he listens when he is beaten.” In Mesopotamia people press cuneiform into wet clay with a reed; Akkadian is the language of letters from Egypt to the Hittites, so Egyptian scribes learn it too. Scholars count in tens and sixties, watch the stars and compile lists of medicines.
primer.ane_p_war.title: Chariots and bows
primer.ane_p_war.text: The striking force of every army is the war chariot: a light car, two horses, a driver and an archer with a powerful composite bow. Charioteers are the elite, called maryannu in the Levant, and each one’s gear costs a fortune. Behind them march infantry with spears, shields and curved khopesh swords. Egypt fights the Hittites, Syrian princes, Nubians and Libyans; Assyria fights Mitanni, Babylon and the Arameans. Campaigns bring back captives, horses and cattle, and the temples take a share of the spoils.
